prompt:
Refine the future theme first into a strong readable headline, a few information lines, and a set of linear structures that can fill the canvas. The first impression of the image must be dominated by extremely heavy, jet-black bold text blocks at the top, cropped close to the edge, pressing down on a large area of fine lines below. The title should look like an architectural beam, not decorative text. The main image should not appear as realistic objects but be translated into multiple groups of horizontal, slightly undulating, manually offset parallel fine lines. Between line groups, there are breaks, intersections, partial tilts, and incomplete alignments, forming an underlying grid where readable order and improvised imbalance coexist. Theme energy intervenes in the line field through scattered paint dots, short smudges, and small color blocks. Colors use a few high-saturation primaries juxtaposed with light gray, pale pink, light blue, green, and orange, resembling traces left after manual splashing or misregistration in printing. Color dots vary greatly in size, ranging from pinpoints to fingertip-sized patches; their distribution seems random but creates pauses, accents, and jumps around the rhythm of the lines. The text system uses extreme compression hierarchy: the main title is a heavy sans-serif black block with wide glyphs, uniform strokes, compressed internal whitespace, flat endpoints, and tight connections. Any writing system should maintain block-face priority and correct character recognition. Auxiliary text is thin, narrow, calm, close to the title or bottom edge, serving as institutionalized information rather than the visual protagonist. The background remains unadorned white paper, retaining clean boundaries, slight printing stiffness, and the imperfection of manual stains. Do not add gradients, shadows, photographic texture, refined illustrations, symmetrical decorations, or softening beautification. Let the black order and colorful accidents together constitute the theme.
